source.title: Is the Number of Trainable Parameters All That Actually Matters?
source.authors: A. Chatelain; Amine Djeghri; Daniel Hesslow; Julien Launay; Iacopo Poli

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out language-model loss against compute while varying the number and type of trainable versus frozen or structured parameters. This is a conceptual test of scaling-law behavior and how it relates to parameter count, rather than a direct reproduction of the original large-scale experiments.
record.gate_note: The text reports a baseline loss-compute exponent and qualitative outcomes for frozen and structured models. Figures 2–7 do not provide extractable numerical curve points in the supplied text, so rows record the text's stated aggregate findings. The cited results from other papers are not recorded as findings. No downstream-task results are reported.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces a loss-versus-compute power-law fit on French autoregressive LMs (exponent −0.041, close to the cited −0.048). It then compares dense models with frozen-parameter and structured-layer variants. This gives direct results on V1 and, through the structured models, on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that frozen random parameters and structured transforms give no loss-compute advantage over dense layers, and that scaling depends only on the actual number of trainable parameters.
record.recipe_differences: The study reports reproducing a loss-compute scaling fit, but uses French data, a different codebase, and relatively small models. It additionally tests frozen-parameter and structured-layer variants rather than only the original dense-model setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The frozen-parameter cost assumption changes the comparison: at two thirds cost the doped models are significantly outperformed by dense baselines, while under a zero-cost assumption their loss-compute curves match models with the same number of trainable parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Frozen random parameters add nothing to the loss-compute curve. At 2/3 cost, doped models are significantly worse than dense baselines. At zero cost, they match dense models with the same trainable count. Structured layers behave according to trainable, not emulated, parameter count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-compute scaling depends on the number of trainable parameters, not on frozen or emulated (structured) parameters.

record.problems: The tested models are small relative to the scale range discussed in the claim. The reported numerical evidence is limited: the baseline exponent is stated, while the comparisons in Figures 2–7 are described qualitatively and individual losses and uncertainty estimates are not given. Experiments use one French training and test setup.
record.rows_left_out: No results were excluded. The figures' individual curve points are not numerically available in the supplied text, so the rows record the authors' stated aggregate outcomes rather than curve-point values.

untested.parts: Separate power laws in parameters or tokens; scale beyond about 10M parameters.
Only two structured variants at one size; no systematic depth/width sweep of dense models.
No comparison of fitting methods or exponent dependence on setup.

record.verdict_notes: The models are tiny (≤9.5M non-embedding parameters in the fit). All variant comparisons are qualitative, from figures, with no numbers or uncertainty. The Figure 1 N values do not map transparently onto the Table 1 size names. This is a workshop paper (ICBINB@NeurIPS).

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss against compute in French autoregressive language models; does not separately test loss against parameter count or tokens, nor all non-bottleneck conditions.
No explicit test of predictions from fits on small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute search for the loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
Tests a limited set of structured and dense architectures; does not establish that architecture details matter little across a wide range of designs.
Only autoregressive language-model pretraining is studied.
Does not compare alternative fitting methods or establish that fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with setup.

rows.subject: GPT-architecture decoder-only autoregressive Transformer baseline models
rows.operation_detail: Measured test loss against compute across model sizes and fit a scaling curve.

conditions.value: 32 billion tokens from Common Crawl filtered by CCNet

rows.measure: Test loss against compute in PF-days; fitted exponent
rows.value: 3.22 · C −0.041; the text states the exponent is −0.041
rows.note: The authors say the exponent is close to −0.048 from cited work. The numerical exponent is stated in the text; individual curve values are not.
rows.check: Correctly linked. The fit spans about four orders of magnitude in compute (1e-7 to 1e-3 PF-days) and models of 100k to 9.5M non-embedding parameters, all far smaller than in the originals.

rows.subject: Doped language models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Doped XSmall, Doped Small, and Doped Medium; exact trainable parameter counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss against compute for models containing frozen random parameters and dense baseline models.

conditions.value: two thirds the cost of trainable parameters
alternating trainable Transformer and frozen MLP layers

rows.baseline: Dense baseline models; their dotted curves are stated to significantly outperform the doped models.
rows.value: Doped models are significantly outperformed by the baseline models.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative comparison across the plotted model family; individual curve values are not stated.
rows.check: This row compares doped models against dense baselines under a 2/3 cost accounting. It does not measure whether loss follows a power law, so 'partial' for V1 is wrong. It concerns which parameters count toward scaling; see fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Doped language models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Doped XSmall, Doped Small, and Doped Medium; exact trainable parameter counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss-compute behavior assuming frozen random parameters have zero cost.
rows.baseline: A model with the same number of trainable parameters and no frozen parameters
rows.value: The doped models reproduce the training curves of a model with the same number of trainable parameters and no frozen parameters; the frozen parameters have no effect on the loss-compute curve.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative finding; individual curve values are not stated.
rows.check: Under an assumed zero cost, doped models match dense models with the same trainable count. This bears on what counts as a parameter, not on whether loss follows a power law. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Structured Adaptive FastFood model
rows.size_stated: 12 layers, dmodel 1024, 16 attention heads; intended to emulate a Small model and reported to perform like an XSmall with a similar number of trainable parameters
rows.operation_detail: Replaced linear layers with adaptive FastFood structured layers and compared loss against compute.

conditions.value: learnable diagonal matrices and Hadamard transforms

rows.measure: Loss against compute and comparison with models having similar trainable parameter counts
rows.baseline: Dense models; the text identifies an XSmall model with a similar number of trainable parameters as the performance comparison.
rows.value: The model intended to emulate a Small performs like an XSmall with a similar number of trainable parameters.
rows.note: Qualitative comparison; individual loss values are not stated.
rows.check: The V1 link is unwarranted, since no power-law fit is reported for this variant. The FastFood model (12 layers, d=1024) matches XSmall (6 layers, d=768) at a similar trainable count. This is consistent with V4 given trainable-parameter count.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1–4.2, Figures 4 and 6; Appendix Tables 1 and 3.

rows.subject: Structured Block Diagonal model
rows.size_stated: 12 layers, dmodel 1024, 16 attention heads; number of blocks set to 4
rows.operation_detail: Replaced the MLP with block diagonal matrices and a block Hadamard transform, then compared loss against compute.

conditions.value: block diagonal matrices and block Hadamard transform

rows.measure: Loss against compute and comparison with models having a similar number of trainable parameters
rows.baseline: Fully trainable models with as many trainable parameters
rows.value: Behavior closely resembles that of a model with as many trainable parameters, despite differences in layer count and model width.
rows.note: Qualitative comparison; individual loss values are not stated.
rows.check: The V1 link is unwarranted. The authors state the behaviour matches a dense model with as many trainable parameters despite different depth and width. This is qualitative only, with no loss values.
